prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identity of its active form, on which incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity was built

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B019 alone, with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. After the full first-round exchange I still find that it is the one shortlisted discovery that has a defined scientific core, a clear change in the field, decades of independent confirmation and outcome-trial evidence at very large scale. I hold it for those reasons and not because six members converge on it; the chair's summary rightly says that convergence settles nothing about attribution. What round 1 changed is how I state the position. The citation should be built on the physiology of GLP-1 and the identity of its active form, with the drugs named as the consequence and not as the object of the prize. The discovery trio is coherent: Holst on gut hormone secretion and incretin physiology, Drucker on proglucagon-derived peptide biology and gut and islet actions, Mojsov on identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide. I would also record in the committee's reasoning that the exclusion of Knudsen is a cost that follows from the three-person limit and from a choice to honour discovery, and is not a judgement that development was unimportant.
statement.case_against: The weak point is documentary, and I cannot close it from the material I am allowed to read. The chair asks which primary publications and dates establish who first showed the activity of GLP-1(7-36) and who first made it. My recollection is that the Mojsov and Habener groups published closely together in the late 1980s, that Mojsov is credited with the identification and synthesis of the truncated active form, and that Habener's contribution is real and outside our credited names. That is recollection, not verified evidence, and I will not let it carry a prize. If the dated record shows Mojsov's role as materially weaker than I recall, the three-person B019 configuration loses its third place without an obvious replacement: Knudsen would turn a discovery citation into a development citation, and a two-person B019 would be an incomplete account. In that case B002, with a compact credit to Walter and Mori, becomes my preferred position. B002 is not a consolation. Its conceptual originality is the strongest on the shortlist, and the only argument against it is that disease relevance is still prospective.

responses.point: The chair asks which configuration each member prefers if the Mojsov priority question cannot be resolved (Drucker, Holst and Mojsov with the dispute stated openly; Drucker, Holst and Knudsen; or a move to B002) and whether any member supports deferring B019 for checking.
responses.response: I propose a threshold in place of a three-way preference. If the dated publications support Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active form as an independent and early contribution, even with a parallel contribution from the Habener group, I would keep Drucker, Holst and Mojsov and say in the reasoning that the credit is shared in time. If the record cannot support that, I would move to B002 and not to Drucker, Holst and Knudsen. The reason is that Knudsen's work is drug development, and a citation built on it no longer describes a discovery in physiology or medicine in the sense I think the prize requires. I do not support deferring B019 so that B002 can wait. B019 is mature now, and the attribution check is something the committee can do before the vote, not a reason for a year's delay.

responses.point: El-Manira moved B019 to the top after ranking B002 first in the opening. She keeps B002 as a fully defensible prize with clean credit and mechanistic originality, and says its still-early clinical translation matters less for a basic-mechanism prize.
responses.response: I agree with you on the last point and I have not claimed that the prize needs a clinical payoff. My case for B019 over B002 rests on a different feature: B019 shows that a discovery in physiology produced a change at the level of patient outcomes, which is the mature end of the arc, while the UPR is a mature mechanism whose consequences for disease are not yet demonstrated. I would not call that a decisive advantage. You raise the question of PERK and ATF6 and whether it weakens Walter and Mori. I think it does not, since Walter and Mori are the discoverers of the pathway and its transcriptional output (IRE1, Hac1/XBP1), and the metazoan branches elaborate it. If our attribution check on Mojsov fails, I will be moving to your first-ranked candidate and not to a compromise.

responses.point: Linnarsson holds Mojsov for the third place because the citation is built on discovery, but says he would openly weigh Knudsen if the Habener dispute proved unresolvable. He also described B019 as the only candidate in everyone's top two.
responses.response: I follow your reasoning on discovery and development and share it, but I would resist the step from an unresolved Habener dispute to Knudsen. Replacing Mojsov with Knudsen would not repair the credit problem, because it would remove the person who identified the active peptide and add the person who developed the drug, which is a different citation and would leave out Habener's side of the discovery in either case. If we cannot hold Mojsov on the record, the honest consequence is that B019 is not ready in this form, not that the third seat goes to the next name. I think that is where you and I differ in degree. If you have evidence that Knudsen's contribution can be described as a discovery in the physiology of GLP-1 and not as drug design, I would like to hear it, since my account of her work does not support that.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked B004 second and B002 last, treats TNF blockade as a mature refinement of an already recognised paradigm, and says Knudsen's omission will be read as favouring academic discovery over development.
responses.response: I accept that the omission will be read that way and I think the committee should say openly what it is doing. I would put the point differently: the prize has often honoured the discovery of the mechanism that makes a drug class possible, and the people who developed the drugs have usually, though not always, been outside it. That tradition is not a principle that makes the exclusion costless, but it is the basis on which I can defend the choice. On B004, you answered my question from round 1 only partly. Every three-person subset of the optogenetics list omits a central contributor, and the same holds for B002 only if one adds the mammalian branches, which I do not think are required for Walter and Mori. I would therefore keep B004 below B002 as a fallback on grounds of credit clarity. We agree on TNF blockade, and it stays out of my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the dated primary record supports Mojsov's identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1 form as an independent early contribution, given the Habener group, who are not on the credited list. I have only recollection.
Whether the committee will accept the exclusion of Knudsen as a consequence of honouring discovery, or will see it as a flaw that should move the committee to B002.
Whether the weight I give to demonstrated outcome benefit over conceptual originality and compact credit (B019 over B002) would survive if a second attribution weakness appeared.
How much the still-accumulating evidence on long-term safety and durability of weight loss should count toward maturity.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. My documented research (nuclear receptors, Nurr1, dopamine neurons) and my past co-authorship with Ronald Evans and Johan Ericson do not involve any credited name on B019, B002, B004 or B008. Co-authorship with Per Svenningsson and Abdel El Manira is disclosed for transparency and concerns no candidate. I do not request a recusal and none is proposed by any other member.
